title: Poner, Salir, Venir --- Completing the -go Club

lessons.title: poner — putting or placing with three singular forms
lessons.gloss: to put or place — with the singular present forms pongo, pones, and pone

segments.text: You already know hago, haces, hace and the careful comparison tengo, hago, digo. Add one verb on its own evidence: poner, “to put” or “to place.”
The g in pongo has the familiar hard sound. Tap the final r of poner lightly; do not turn it into the stronger written rr sound.

poner descends from Latin pōnere, “to put or place.” English keeps the same placing family in position, compose (“place together”), and deposit (“place down”). The two shapes pon- and pos- are historical relatives, so poner and position are cousins even though their endings differ.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: only the three singular forms

utterances: person: yo. present of poner: pongo.
person: tú. present of poner: pones.
person: él / ella / usted. present of poner: pone.

segments.text: Say the bounded set as pongo, pones, pone. The learned yo form joins the known comparison because it ends in -go. That resemblance helps memory; it still does not predict an unseen verb.

For now, practise the forms and their meaning without importing a new object. Later lessons can add the nouns needed for expressions such as setting a table or putting on clothing. Plural persons and reflexive ponerse also wait.

lessons.title: salir — leaving with three singular forms
lessons.gloss: to leave or go out — with the singular present forms salgo, sales, and sale

segments.text: You can retrieve pongo, pones, pone, and you already use de with a place name. Keep that frontier while adding salir, “to leave” or “to go out.”
The g in salgo is hard. Keep the l clear in every form: salgo, sales, sale.

salir descends from Latin salīre, “to leap” or “to jump.” The older image of leaping outward developed into the everyday meaning “to go out.” English salient first carried the sense “leaping” or “springing,” and a sally is a sudden movement outward. Those cousins preserve the same motion without requiring a long list of uncertain relatives.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: one more singular set

utterances: person: yo. present of salir: salgo.
person: tú. present of salir: sales.
person: él / ella / usted. present of salir: sale.

segments.text: Say salgo, sales, sale. Only the learned yo form contains g. Compare it with pongo because both forms are now known, not because one form could have predicted the other.
Reuse the known word de and the familiar place name Madrid:
Salgo de Madrid. — “I leave Madrid.”
Sales de Madrid. — “You leave Madrid.”
Sale de Madrid. — “He, she, or formal you leaves Madrid.”
Plural persons, dating expressions, house vocabulary, and the noun for “exit” wait until their own lessons.

lessons.title: venir — coming with three singular forms
lessons.gloss: to come — with the singular present forms vengo, vienes, and viene

segments.text: You can say salgo de Madrid, and you already know tengo, tienes, tiene. Now learn venir, “to come,” inside exactly the same three singular persons.
The g in vengo is hard. In vienes and viene, let ie move as one smooth vowel sequence.

venir descends from Latin venīre, “to come.” English convene means “come together”; an event is something that “comes out”; and adventure passed through the idea of what may “come to” a person. The recurring ven- or vent- shape marks this old coming family.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: one known comparison, still singular

utterances: person: yo. present of venir: vengo. known tener comparison: tengo.
person: tú. present of venir: vienes. known tener comparison: tienes.
person: él / ella / usted. present of venir: viene. known tener comparison: tiene.

segments.text: Say vengo, vienes, viene. The learned singular forms line up closely with tengo, tienes, tiene: the yo form ends in -go, while the other two show ie. This comparison describes two complete learned sets; it does not introduce a plural “boot” table or license guesses about other verbs.
Now contrast leaving and coming with known de and Madrid:
Salgo de Madrid. — “I leave Madrid.”
Vengo de Madrid. — “I come from Madrid.”
Vienes de Madrid. — “You come from Madrid.”
Plural persons and free-standing arrival vocabulary wait for later lessons.

lessons.title: Practice — putting, leaving, and coming in the singular
lessons.gloss: singular putting, leaving, and coming, plus the six learned yo forms

segments.text: This checkpoint adds nothing. Retrieve the three bounded singular sets first. Only then widen the memory comparison from three learned yo forms to six.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the complete Chapter 13 frame

segments.text: putting or placing: pongo, pones, pone.
leaving or going out: salgo, sales, sale.
coming: vengo, vienes, viene.
known-word contrast: Salgo de Madrid. Vengo de Madrid.
known singular comparison: vengo / tengo, vienes / tienes, viene / tiene.

Now that all three new verbs have been taught, the learned yo comparison can grow to exactly tengo, hago, digo, pongo, salgo, vengo. It remains a retrieval aid, not a rule for predicting any unseen verb.
Plural persons, full boot diagrams, reflexive clothing expressions, house and table nouns, clock times, dinner vocabulary, and other unseen contexts remain outside this checkpoint.

blocks.title: The words, taken apart — retrieve the history

segments.text: poner continues Latin pōnere, the placing family of position.
salir continues Latin salīre, the leaping family of salient.
venir continues Latin venīre, the coming family of convene.
different inherited histories and analogy let the six known yo forms converge on -go; the shared shape does not make a productive prediction rule.
